paper_title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

Most cultural benchmarks assess whether models possess cultural knowledge (Hu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; AlKhamissi et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Chowdhury et al., 2025). However, cultural understanding also requires applying it to infer implicit meanings from contextual cues, and as LLMs gain greater knowledge and stronger reasoning, their failures increasingly come from choosing the wrong interpretation rather than lacking the fact (Gekhman et al., 2026). Riddles could test this ability, particularly compositional and abductive reasoning (Halder et al., 2026). They have long served to test cultural understanding in traditions from ancient Greece, Rome, and India to China (Szalc, 2011; Tan et al., 2016; Monda, 2016), and they span topics from history and politics to sports and literature (Kaivola-Bregenhøj, 2018). Solving cultural riddle requires weighing alternative cultural associations for each clue, combining them into coherent whole (compositional reasoning), and inferring the answer that best explains all clues (abductive reasoning) (Halder et al., 2026). E.g., as shown in Table 1, the German riddle requires interpreting the German 9/11 in German daymonth order, then recalling the historical events and name of 9 November. By contrast, simply asking What is 9 November called in Germany? would require only factual recall. Cultural riddles thus test whether LLMs can interpret cultural clues and combine knowledge with reasoning. Cultural riddles have been benchmarked for few languages (Fabbri et al., 2025; Boczka, 2026; Sayeedi et al., 2026; Minggad et al., 2026), where they challenge even frontier LLMs. However, existing cultural benchmarks have three key limitations: (L1) narrow linguistic and geographic coverage, (L2) insuﬀicient validation of data quality and diﬀiculty, and (L3) the lack of robust, scalable, human-informed evaluation protocol. We address these limitations with CULTURALRIDDLES, benchmark of 6,191 original riddles written by community members in their own languages. CULTURALRIDDLES spans 62 communities in 51 languages and 45 countries. It includes languages absent from prior cultural benchmarks, and many-to-many links between languages and countries, such as seven languages in multiple countries and seven countries with multiple languages. (L1, Figure 2). Native speakers other than the author verify every riddle (L2). We benchmark 28 proprietary and open model configurations and, to our knowledge, conduct the largest and most multilingual human evaluation of model answers to open-ended cultural knowledge tasks: native speakers labeled 68,067 unique answers across 57 communities in 48 languages, covering 59.10% of 170,520 model responses; rulebased scoring and two human-validated LLM judges score most remaining responses, with unresolved cases excluded from accuracy (L3). Our results reveal substantial cultural gaps: the best model achieves 79.4% overall accuracy, yet no model exceeds 22% in the Lumasaba and Mongondow communities. Translating riddles from five of the hardest communities into English closes only about one-fifth of the accuracy gap to high-resource communities, suggesting that language barriers alone do not explain these differences. We also find that exact-match scoring misses many valid answers and alters model rankings, highlighting the importance of human-informed evaluation. Through riddles written and reviewed by community members, CULTURALRIDDLES offers nuanced assessment of how well current models can solve original, culturally grounded riddles in their respective languages, probing lived experience and locally specific knowledge beyond well-documented facts. The benchmark can also grow to include new communities and track model progress over time.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Cultural Benchmarks Cultural benchmarks for LLMs mostly operationalize culture as knowledge, norms and values, social dynamics, or bias (Adilazuarda et al., 2024; AlKhamissi et al., 2026). For example, BLEnD (Myung et al., 2024), CulturalBench (Chiu et al., 2025), and CVQA (Romero et al., 2024) test everyday cultural knowledge, while NormAd (Rao et al., 2025) and WorldValuesBench (Zhao et al., 2024) probe social norms and values. These benchmarks are mostly closed-form and test recognition or recall, which says little about whether models apply cultural knowledge when reasoning (Zhou et al., 2025). Global PIQA (Chang et al., 2025), CulturALL (Lin et al., 2026), and Macaron (Elsetohy et al., 2026) combine cultural knowledge with multi-step reasoning, and CultureForest (Ye et al., 2026) requires models to apply culturally grounded norms. While some cultural QA benchmarks include human evaluation, they do so at small scale (120700 answers evaluated across <10 languages) (Myung et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2025; Hasan et al., 2025; Libovický et al., 2026). Overall, existing benchmarks vary widely in coverage and in how much content is written and evaluated by humans  (Table 2)  . Riddle Benchmarks General riddle benchmarks test commonsense and lateral thinking predominantly in English: RiddleSense (Lin et al., 2021), BrainTeaser (Jiang et al., 2023b), and BiRdQA (Zhang & Wan, 2022) use multiple-choice riddles and puzzles, and RiddleBench (Halder et al., 2026) collects logic puzzles from exam papers; Chinese character riddles (Tan et al., 2016) add wordplay. They rarely require cultural knowledge. Cultural riddle benchmarks exist only for few languages or locales. In MultiNRC (Fabbri et al., 2025), 258 out of 1,055 reasoning questions are wordplay and riddles; no model exceeds 50% on LLM judge scores. BanglaRiddleEval (Sayeedi et al., 2026) features 1,244 traditional Bangla riddles with LLM-generated explanations and distractors; the best multiple-choice accuracy is about 56%, against 83% for humans. MonCulture-eval (Minggad et al., 2026) includes Mongolian riddle task across two scripts and three regions, scored by LLM judges with human audit of 10% of the scores. Boczka (2026) introduced riddle writing focused on culture-specific associations and clues across list of selected topics, with an evaluation scheme focused on hallucinations and abstention. Each of the existing cultural riddle benchmarks covers one to three languages with one locale per language, relies on multiple choice, unvalidated LLM judges, or human scoring alone, and covers few topics and model families. CULTURALRIDDLES scales the one-language pilot of Boczka (2026) to 62 communities, with human and validated LLM-judge evaluation.

sections.title: 3 CulturalRiddles Benchmark
sections.content: CULTURALRIDDLES contains 6,191 original riddles written by 167 native speakers for 62 national-linguistic communities. The target is 100 riddles per community: ten for each of eight shared topics, which enable cross-cultural comparison, and ten for each of two topics chosen by the community1.

sections.title: 3.1 Participatory Benchmark Construction
sections.content: Community Unit & Recruiting Neither language nor country alone captures cultural context, so our working unit is the national-linguistic community as it exists today (e.g., Hungarian in Hungary, Spanish in Mexico), an imperfect (AlKhamissi et al., 2026) but scalable basis for data collection and coverage reporting. We recruited volunteer writers through social media and personal networks, requiring only self-identification with community, proficiency in its language, and basic English. Over six months, 167 writers contributed, typically one or two per community (App. A.1). Consent to publish the data was obtained from the writers, and all participants are offered opportunities to contribute to research on top of the collected data. 1The 6,191 released riddles exclude eight removed for harmful or discriminatory content and one excluded from human evaluation for using wrong language. 5 Figure 2: Cultural riddles across languages and borders. CULTURALRIDDLES brings together 6,191 original riddles from 62 communities across 51 languages and 45 countries, including many underrepresented languages and locales. See App. A.1 for the full list. Task Format and Example Each riddle instance contains topic, an indirectly phrased riddle, and short reference answer in the local language, with optional hints and comments  (Table 1)  . Most instances also include English translations, which serve only as reading aids: they may lose information needed to solve the riddle and some concepts simply have no English equivalent. Riddle Writing Process & Instructions Each team wrote its riddles from scratch within the shared topic framework, without translating content from other communities. Writers were asked for tricky, indirect questions with single exact answer (typically 14 words), using synonyms, indirect descriptions, local jargon, and nicknames recognizable within their community, so that solving riddle takes more than single lookup or web search. In post-writing survey (76 respondents from 43 communities), 97.4% of respondents reported having drawn on personal knowledge and experience, 68.4% also on online sources, and 55.3% on other community members. To calibrate diﬀiculty, 46.1% tested riddles on AI tools (without revealing the answers); 39.5% used AI to brainstorm and 5.3% to paraphrase or co-write. Quality & Diversity Assurance At least one native speaker other than the author verifies every riddle: it must be solvable, its clues unambiguous, and its reference answer correct. Not every community member must be able to solve it, since some riddles rely on knowledge specific to generation, region, or interest (Boczka, 2026), and agreement is not requirement for cultural truth (AlKhamissi et al., 2026). In our survey, one third of riddle writers estimated their riddles would mostly rely on only well-known knowledge, another third also included some regional knowledge, 26% mostly regional or local knowledge, and only 3% estimated they would require niche knowledge.

sections.title: 3.2 Contents and Coverage
sections.content: Linguistic and Geographic Coverage CULTURALRIDDLES (Figure 2) includes languages absent from prior cultural benchmarks (e.g., Buginese, Mongondow, Masaaba, Konkani, Sudanese Arabic) and underrepre6 Figure 3: Communities favor different riddle forms. Share of riddles in each form, overall (6,092 English translations, 61 communities) and in one community dominated by each form, labeled by ISO 639-3 language and ISO 3166 country code  (Table 5)  . Questions end in ? or open with question word (WH-questions open with one); first-person riddles contain first-person pronoun. sented locales (e.g., Uganda, Luxembourg, Cuba). Its languagecountry mapping is denser than in prior benchmarks  (Table 2)  : seven languages appear in several countries (e.g., Spanish in Argentina, Cuba, Peru, and Spain), seven countries contribute several languages (e.g., ten for India), and Arabic appears in five varieties. Topics Building on the Hungarian riddles of Boczka (2026), we selected eight shared topics expected to be relevant across cultures (Politics, History, Geography, Arts, Sports, National Heritage, Kids World, and Everyday Life). Additionally, each community could freely choose two wildcard topics, designated to capture particularly relevant concepts of their culture. Among the 124 topics chosen by communities, the most common theme is Food (27.4%), followed by Nature (15.3%), Language (13.7%), and Media (12.9%). We also received culture-exclusive topics, such as Public bath etiquette by Japanese (Japan) and Wedding Micro-traditions by Sindhi (India) communities. Writers rated Politics the hardest shared topic to write (3.41/5) and Everyday Life the easiest (2.37/5). Riddle Patterns & Content We imposed no fixed format on the riddles to leave room for unique cultural preferences. The examples in Table 1 illustrate the diversity of riddle formats chosen, e.g., brief statement in the German and Luxembourgish examples or first-person description in the Sudanese Arabic example. Many communities favor one form: 98% of Luganda riddles close with first-person question (Who am I?), while 98% of Japanese riddles close with short question of the type What is it? (Figure 3). Some riddles also build on the cultures own riddle traditions, e.g., Tamil riddles about Geography grounded in old Tamil poetry about landscapes, or Persian riddles built on wordplay, poetic imagery, and rhyme. Many others draw on collective memory, including painful histories (e.g., betrayal at Plassey (Bangladesh), persecution under Brazils dictatorship, imprisonment and survival in Syria, or the contradiction between slavery and ideals of equality in the US). These clues reach beyond language into shared ways of remembering: particularly in Politics and History, few words can evoke larger narrative of loss, injustice, or resistance. Solving them requires familiarity with how an event is remembered, not only with the event itself. Data and code. CULTURALRIDDLES is available on Hugging Face under CC-BY-4.0, with the request that it not be used to train models or to generate synthetic data. Code for evaluation and analysis is available at https://github.com/Cohere-Labs-Community/CulturalRiddles. New communities can contribute through the repository, which provides riddle template, an automatic format check, and review process.

sections.title: 4.1 Models
sections.content: We evaluate 28 proprietary, open-weight, and open-source model configurations (Figure 6)2. They are dense and mixture-of-experts models with disclosed sizes from 0.8B to 1.6T parameters, several reasoning settings, and one search-enabled configuration. Each configuration answers the 6,090 benchmarked riddles (61 communities) once with the same English prompt template including country and topic for context (App. A.2), yielding 170,520 total responses3.

sections.title: 4.2 Evaluation
sections.content: Metric Each answer receives score of 0 (incorrect), 1 (admits not knowing), 2 (partially correct), or 3 (correct). To capture finer distinctions within these score categories, we define 13 response types, such as hallucinated (score 0) and different valid answer (score 3), as shown in Tables 3 and 4. Our primary metric, accuracy, is the share of scored responses with score 3. Accuracy differences are reported in percentage points (pp). Scoring Pipeline Open-ended answers may differ from the reference while remaining correct. To balance reliability and annotation effort, each of the 170,520 responses takes one of three routes to score (Figure 4): rules, native speakers, or human-validated LLM jury. sections.title: 5 Results
sections.content: We first assess whether the jury agrees with native speakers (Section 5.1), then compare models and communities using combined rule, human, and jury scores (Sections 5.2, 5.3 and 5.5) over the 57 communities with valid human evaluation. Error-type analyses use only rule-based scores and human labels (Section 5.4).

sections.title: 5.1 LLM judge agreement approaches human agreement
sections.content: Human annotators agree on scores but less on error types. On the doubly annotated sample (setting A, Figure 5), humans agree on accuracy at Cohens κ = 0.80 0.04 and on the 03 score at quadratic-weighted κ = 0.80 0.03 (Landis & Koch, 1977). Accuracy agreement ranges across communities from κ = 0.59 (Ukrainian) to 1.00 (Luganda), excluding two communities with too few correct answers. Agreement on the 13 error types is weaker (κ = 0.41 with partial credit within score, 0.31 without), mostly because the guideline left room for subjective interpretation: hallucinated versus right category, wrong entity, when to award partial credit, and whether different valid answer needs its own label rather than correct. We therefore use error types descriptively (Section A.3). LLMhuman agreement is comparable to humanhuman agreement. In setting A, individual zeroshot judges agree with H1 and H2 at κ = 0.790.81 on accuracy and quadratic-weighted κ = 0.790.83 on the 03 score, close to humanhuman agreement on both. Agreement with H1 remains high in setting B: 0.830.84 on accuracy and 0.820.83 on scores. Like humans, judges agree less on fine-grained response types (0.380.52). Human disagreement is more frequent when judges disagree. The two LLM judges agree highly on accuracy in all three settings (Figure 5). In setting A, humans disagree on accuracy for 27% of pairs where the judges disagree, 8.4 times the rate where they agree, and on the full 03 score for 39%, 5.1 times the rate where they agree. First, they are lenient on the strongest models: they jointly accept 9.0% and 6.9% of human-rejected answers from Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5, respectively (Figure 15). Second, they reject valid alternatives: individual judges reject 25 29% of different valid answers, versus about 5% of answers labeled simply correct. Third, agreement varies across communities, ranging from κ = 0.65 for Swahili to 0.98 for Belarusian and Catalan (Figure 16).

sections.content: Larger models generally perform better, but not always Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview leads at 79.4%, followed by GPT-5.5 (76.3%) and Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking (66.0%; Figure 6). The best open model, DeepSeek V4 Pro with high reasoning, ranks fifth at 63.8%. Apart from other configurations of these models and Gemini 2.5 Flash (50.1%), every model scores below 40%, and models of 8B parameters or fewer reach at most 12 Figure 7: Even the strongest models struggle in the hardest communities. Color indicates language-resource levels defined by Common Crawl page counts (Figure 8); marker shapes indicate native-speaker review coverage among responses for each model routed beyond automatic rules (App. A.4.0.9). 10.4%. Yet size alone does not explain performance: Gemma 4 31B (39.6%) outperforms both the similarly sized OLMo-3 32B Think (11.3%) and the larger Apertus 70B models (15.2% and 19.6%). Regional models show no extra advantage in their target regions. We test whether regionally adapted models gain more in their target regions than elsewhere. Regional Tiny Aya variants do not differ significantly within any region (Cochrans Q, all > 0.48). Qwen-SEA-LION-4.5 27B gains 5.5 pp over Qwen3.5 27B overall, but we find no significant extra gain in its target regions. Reasoning helps, but web search can hurt. Thinking raises Claude Opus 4.7s accuracy by 6.3 pp, and high reasoning effort adds 5.0 pp for DeepSeek V4 Pro. Web search, by contrast, lowers GPT-5.5s accuracy by 11.8 pp. Among answers that GPT-5.5 gives correctly without search but incorrectly with it and that humans assigned an error type, 39% name the wrong entity in the right category and 25% are hallucinated. Search may reinforce familiar keyword associations: Swahili (Kenya) riddle asks for the home of the Lunatic Express, but multiple models return the Uganda Railway itself. They identify the entity associated with Lunatic Express while overlooking home, which points to the intended Railway Museum in Nairobi.

sections.title: 5.3 Exact match misses half of correct answers
sections.content: Exact match credits only responses matching the reference answer (case-insensitive), missing about 47% of responses ultimately scored correct across the human-evaluated communities (Figure 6). Among the 132,940 responses scored by rules or humans, native speakers judged an additional 9.51% correct without subtype recorded and labeled 6.16% as different valid answers  (Table 3)  . Human and jury review raises accuracy by 64166% relative to exact match for every model except Qwen3.5 0.8B, whose larger relative gain (213%) reflects very small exact-match count. Gains generally grow toward weaker models, so exact match can exaggerate performance gaps and change rankings; for example, Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking moves from fifth to third after review.

sections.title: 5.4 Models hallucinate rather than abstain
sections.content: The most frequent error across riddles is hallucinated answer, one that is made up or unrelated to the riddle (24.19% of the 132,940 responses scored by rules or humans). In contrast, only 0.80% of these responses admit not knowing, even though the prompt asks models to answer dont know when they do not know (Figure 10). Hallucinations shrink as accuracy rises (Figure 12 in App. B.1), but abstention stays rare for every model (at most 3.81% for any model).

sections.title: 5.5 High averages hide cultural blind spots
sections.content: Most models agree on what is easy. The eight easiest communitiesEnglish (USA), Japanese, French (France), Portuguese (Brazil), Dutch, English (Canada), Malay, and French (Canada)have mean accuracies of 4766% across models, and seven of them use high-resource languages (Figure 7), defined by Common Crawl page counts (Figure 8). At least 20 of 28 models exceed 20% accuracy in each, and the median model reaches 73% on English (USA), plausibly because these cultures are well documented on the web and hence in LLM training data. African and Indonesian communities challenge every model. The eight hardest communities are Swahili (Kenya), Afaan Oromo, Luganda, Yoruba, Sudanese Arabic, Lumasaba, Buginese, and Mongondow (mean accuracy 414%; Figure 7). Here 1525 of 28 models score below 10%, and the median model scores only 09%. Even Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-5.5 average just 43% and 39% across these eight, about half their overall accuracy. No model exceeds 22% on Lumasaba or Mongondow. Low-resource languages increase the challenge. Six of the eight hardest communities use lowor extremely low-resource languages (fewer than 100K pages in Common Crawl). Across all human-evaluated communities, pooled accuracy falls from 37.0% for high-resource languages to 30.8% for medium, 18.0% for low, and 12.7% for extremely low-resource languages (Figure 8), yet community accuracies still vary with standard deviation of 813 pp within each level. Swahili is medium-resource, and Sudanese Arabic inherits the high-resource classification of Arabic: neither escapes the hardest group.

sections.title: 6 Analysis
sections.content: We first examine what makes riddle diﬀicult and how language contributes (Section 6.1), then pose the riddles as crosswords (Section 6.2), and finally estimate the effort of evaluating new models (Section 6.3).

sections.title: 6.1 What makes a riddle difficult?
sections.content: Diﬀiculty mostly comes from the riddle, then the language. To separate model ability from riddle diﬀiculty, we fit crossed random-effects logistic model (Bates et al., 2015) to 129,928 scored responses from modelcommunity pairs with at most 2% unscored responses. Here, variance measures the spread in the estimated likelihood of correct answer on the models latent log-odds scale. Model identity accounts for 38% of the total variance (Figure 9). Among the components associated with the benchmark rather than the answering model, individual riddles account for about 60%, language 24%, community within language 13%, and topic 2%. Models largely agree on which languages and communities are hard: interactions between model identity and benchmark factors account for less than 2% of total variance. Riddle features explain only 3.1% of the riddle-level variance (App. B.2), but rare answer terms matter. About 14 Figure 8: Language resources do not explain all community differences. For example, the Konkani riddle Layers of sweet, made during Christmas, what is this? asks for bebinca, but GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 Thinking answer kuswar, the platter of Goan Christmas sweets that includes it. They identify the dish family but miss the specific dish. Language coverage is not community coverage. Language resources remain associated with accuracy after accounting for model identity and riddle features, consistent with the resource disparities documented by Joshi et al. (2020) and the cross-language gaps in INCLUDE (Romanou et al., 2025). In our feature model, the adjusted odds of correct answer for lowand extremely low-resource languages are 0.10 (95% CI 0.02 0.48) and 0.04 (0.010.15) times those for high-resource languages, so high-resource riddle has roughly 10 and 25 times the odds. The medium-resource estimate (0.49, 0.201.21) is less certain (App. B.2). 15 Even among communities sharing both language and script, accuracy differs by 526 pp (App. B.2). For example, Simplified Chinese (China) averages 28.5% versus 46.3% for Chinese (Singapore), gap of 17.8 pp. Language-level averages thus conceal differences between the communities that multilingual model is meant to serve. Translating into English helps, but does not close the gap. To estimate how much of this diﬀiculty comes from language alone, we benchmark five models (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.7, DeepSeek V4 Pro, Qwen-SEA-LION-4.5 27B) on English translations of the riddles from five hardest communities (Section 5.5). After excluding 41 translations that contain the full reference answer as clue (e.g., am the art of making pottery for pottery; 38 from Lumasaba), 458 riddles remain; English responses are scored by rules and the LLM jury without native-speaker review (App. B.4). On the 2,049 responses scored in both conditions, accuracy rises from 22.1% to 32.4% (paired gain +10.3 pp, 95% CI 7.613.0; Figure 14). Buginese, Lumasaba, and Yoruba gain 1418 pp, while Sudanese Arabic shows no detectable gain. The same models reach about 69% on high-resource communities, so translation closes only about fifth of the gap: much of the diﬀiculty persists in English.

sections.title: 6.2 Beyond open-ended answers: Crosswords
sections.content: Because each riddle has short, exact answer, CULTURALRIDDLES can also be posed in other formats. We pose the riddles as crosswords, long-standing testbed for language models (Wallace et al., 2022; Saha et al., 2025; Leng et al., 2025), which adds checkable constraints: each answer must fit its slot and share letters with the answers that cross it. We built 53 text grids from the communities riddle submissions (5,057 entries)4 and gave the same clues to 11 model configurations in five matched conditions: plain batch, batch with answer lengths, lengths plus quarter of each answers letters, crossword with list output, and crossword with grid output. We compare crossword input with the length condition, so that both see the same lengths (App. B.3). Crossing structure changes reference agreement by only +1.6 points (95% CI 0.3 to 3.7), but raises the share of consistent crossings from 53.0% to 60.1% (+7.2, 4.89.6): the answers agree more with each other without matching the references more often. Filling the grid is separate skill that varies widely between models: Gemini 3.7 Flash scores 75.6% with list output but 5.4% with grid output, Claude Opus 4.8 returns no usable grid for any puzzle, and GPT-6 Astra places 88.3% of answers correctly.

sections.title: 6.3 Effort of benchmarking new models
sections.content: We recommend scoring new model on CULTURALRIDDLES in four steps, each passing fewer answers onward: (1) rules for exact matches, empty outputs, placeholders, and explicit admissions of not knowing (18.87% of our responses); (2) existing human labels for answers already given to the same riddle; (3) the LLM jury, which keeps score only when both judges agree; and (4) native speakers for unresolved answers, with extra review in communities where agreement with human labels is low (Swahili (Kenya);App. A.4). Treating each model as new and using only rules and human labels from the other models (App. B.5), these steps already cover about 80% of the leading models responses, since strong models tend to repeat answers that other models gave. Coverage falls to 51% for the median model and 213% for the smallest models, whose answers are mostly unique. Roughly 100115 answers per leading model would still need native review. 4Chinese varieties, Thai, Kannada, and Buginese were excluded because their grids could not be built reliably.

sections.title: 7 Discussion & Conclusion
sections.content: We built CULTURALRIDDLES, participatory benchmark of 6,191 original riddles from 62 communities (45 countries, 51 languages), to test how LLMs combine cultural knowledge with reasoning. Native speakers write, verify, and score its riddles, recognizing answers that exact match misses and judges sometimes reject. Frontier models lead overall, yet the top three proprietary configurations each score below 50% in 69 of the 57 human-evaluated communities, and the best open configuration does so in 11. No model exceeds 22% on Lumasaba or Mongondow. Models rarely admit not knowing. Evaluations that treat abstentions and wrong answers alike can reward guessing (Kalai et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025); our 03 scale tracks abstention alongside accuracy. Translation closes only fifth of the hardest communities gap to high-resource communities, communities sharing language and script differ by up to 26 pp, and regional adaptation shows no detectable extra advantage in its target regions. Stronger multilingual ability alone is therefore unlikely to close these gaps; much of what models lack appears to be content from the communities themselves. The largest diﬀiculty lies in what the riddles are built on: associations, traditions, perceptions, and memories shared within community. Community members write and verify these riddles, so this knowledge is available to them by construction, yet the best models still miss it in many communities; final-answer scores cannot show whether they lack facts or misread clues. Because scoring needs native-speaker review for only about 100 answers per leading model (Section 6.3), CULTURALRIDDLES can grow to new models and communities and track how far future models move this cultural frontier.

sections.title: 8 Ethics Statement
sections.content: Riddle writers and annotators are members of the communities they represent and contributed as unpaid volunteers. All contributors joined under project proposal that described CULTURALRIDDLES as an open benchmark to be released publicly; follow-up form asked the authors how they wish to be credited. The released dataset credits writers at the community level and does not attribute individual riddles. We report the writer survey only in aggregate. Some riddles refer to painful histories, such as persecution, dictatorship, or slavery. We keep them because they are part of how these communities remember events. After content review, we removed 8 riddles and added content note to 56 others; the dataset card includes content disclaimer. The data released contains no names or contact details of contributors.

sections.content: A.1 Benchmark Coverage Table 5 lists the communities in CULTURALRIDDLES, each identified by language and country. A.2 Benchmarking Prompt and Models All models receive the prompt in Figure 10. Open-weight and open-source models range from 0.8B to 1.6T parameters and include general multilingual and reasoning families (Qwen (Qwen Team, 2026), Gemma (Gemma Team et al., 2025), Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023a), OLMo (Team Olmo et al., 2025)) and models built for multilingual or regional coverage (Tiny Aya (Salamanca et al., 2026), EuroLLM (Ramos et al., 2026), Apertus (Hernández-Cano et al., 2026; Project Apertus et al., 2026), SEA-LION (Ng et al., 2025)). Proprietary models include GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026), Claude Opus 4.7 (Anthropic, 2026), and Gemini 3.1 (Google DeepMind, 2026), with their reasoning and web-search variants (Figure 6). Compute. The runs used about 217M tokens in total (119M input, 98M output; one batch of 1,700 Gemini 3.1 Pro answers has no token counts). Inputs average 455730 tokens per riddle (about 1,700 for GPT-5.5 and 4,900 with web search, including retrieved context). Outputs range from about 70 tokens per riddle (Gemma 4, Nova) to 6,700 (OLMo-3 Think). Because runs mixed hosted APIs and locally served models, we report tokens rather than cost. Limitations of single runs. Each configuration answered each riddle once with one prompt, so rankings could change under prompt variations (Mizrahi et al., 2024), and scores might not be reproducible under stochastic decoding. A.3 Human Evaluation Protocol Procedure. culturally specific riddle benchmark. Output Requirements Return ONLY valid JSON object. You are solving cultural riddle from {community_display}. The riddle is written in {community_display} ({script_name}), and its topic is {topic}. Use this cultural and linguistic context to interpret the riddle, reason about its clues, and provide your final answer. NEVER output any text before or after the JSON object. Do NOT use double quotes () inside the riddle_answer or reasoning values, as they will break the JSON. If you need to quote something, use single quotes () instead. Input Format Output Template The riddle is provided as plain text on the line(s) following RIDDLE: marker: RIDDLE: <the riddle text> Input Example RIDDLE: speak without mouth and hear without ears. have no body, but come alive with wind. What am I? Instructions Read the riddle carefully. Use both the content of the riddle and any relevant cultural knowledge associated with the specified community. Provide the answer you believe is most likely correct, and write your answer in {community_display} ({script_name}). If you do not know the answer, return dont know as the riddle_answer. Do not invent an answer simply to be responsive. Your reasoning should be brief (12 sentences), explaining the key clues you used and why you selected the answer. If uncertain, briefly state what information is missing or why the riddle is ambiguous. { } riddle_answer: <your_riddle_answer>, reasoning: <your_reasoning_in_1_2_sentences> Output Example { riddle_answer: an echo, reasoning: The riddle describes something that speaks without mouth and is heard without ears, which points to an echo. } Figure 10: The benchmarking prompt used for all models. Placeholders in braces are filled per riddle with its specific context, e.g. Konkani, India for community_display and Devanagari script for script_name. 29 scored by rules and 192 pairs from prompt-development riddles. Human correctness agreement ranges from κ = 0.59 (Ukrainian) to 1.00 (Luganda), excluding two communities with too few correct answers for stable estimate. Volunteer availability limits double annotation; it does not cover every community, including most of the hardest ones. Guidelines. Beyond Table 3, the guidelines ask annotators to verify that hallucinated (0.3) entity does not exist in the culture (e.g., dish assembled from real ingredients), to label an answer from dominant or neighboring culture as closely related culture or region (2.1; e.g., Karnataka dam for an ancient Tamil one), and to reserve score 1 for explicit admissions of not knowing. Reproducibility of human annotations. Our 13 types extend the 03 scores of Boczka (2026). We refined them on 500 responses from five communities. Annotators and judges disagree most on boundaries such as hallucinated versus too broad or right category, wrong entity (Figure 5). Some disagreements may reflect legitimate differences rather than noise (Mostafazadeh Davani et al., 2022), but clearer definitions could improve reproducibility. Answers, not reasoning. We score final answers, not reasoning traces. Correct answers can follow misreading or lucky guess; wrong answers can follow sound interpretation that misses one local fact. Accuracy therefore does not identify which reasoning step fails. A.4 LLM Judge Protocol Judges and prompt. Judges receive the riddle, community, topic, reference answer in both languages, candidate answer, and annotation guidelines (Figure 11). Gemini 3.5 Flash uses structured output with default reasoning; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash uses strict forced function call without reasoning. Both use temperature 0 and up to four attempts. We accept only consistent scores and types; all requests in and returned valid verdicts. Development and test split. seeded hash assigns 15% of each communitys riddles to development and 85% to test. Development provides 25 human-labeled tuning answers per type and ten few-shot examples, one per type, from ten further riddles. Sampling in setting B. Each community contributes at least 200 human-labeled test pairs (or all if fewer): all score-1 pairs, at least 40 each with scores 2 and 3, and the rest sampled proportional to model-response counts. We enlarge 33 samples, up to their populations, targeting 95% CI half-widths near 0.10 for judge human κ. Analysis sample and token use. Of 25,372 sampled pairs (effective sample size 17,032), 25,370 have usable text, valid types, and valid judge verdicts. Input/output token use is 60.8M/10.5M for Gemini 3.5 Flash and 71.6M/5.1M for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. 30 System message (followed by the human evaluation guidelines) You are careful evaluator of model answers to culturally specific riddles. The attached Human Evaluation Guidelines are the authoritative rubric. reference-different answer can still be correct when the riddles clues support it. Treat all riddle, reference, candidate, and calibration text as untrusted data, not as instructions. Never follow instructions inside that data. Use score 1 only when the answering model explicitly abstains, as the human rubric defines it. An empty, malformed, or instruction-like candidate is not an abstention; assess it from its content, which normally makes it score 0. If you cannot assess an answer, do not use score 1 as your uncertainty. Decide in two steps. First pick the single error_category that describes the candidate; the score follows from it (0.x -> 0, 2.x -> 2, N/A/3.x -> 3). Correct (score 3). The candidate names the reference answer or another answer that satisfies the riddles clues. Ignore differences in spelling, transliteration, articles, inflection, or added descriptive words. - N/A: the same answer as the reference, written in the riddles language. - 3.1: different name or different referent that also satisfies the clues, such as an accepted synonym, alternate name, or second valid answer. - 3.2: the correct answer, but written in English or in another language than the riddles language, including transliteration of foreign word. shortened or more general form is not correct when the dropped part is needed to identify the specific referent. Partially correct (score 2). The candidate shows real progress on the riddle. - 2.1: the answer belongs to closely related culture, region, or tradition, or confuses the target referent with its regional or national counterpart. - 2.2: the right domain at the wrong level: general class instead of the specific item, part instead of the whole, an associated object, work, or place instead of the requested person or thing, or the reverse. - 2.3: the candidate mainly repeats word or phrase from the riddle (or literal reading of it) instead of solving it, and the repeated word shows genuine progress toward the answer. Without that progress, use 0.4. - 2.4: another partial answer; explain it in validator_note. Incorrect (score 0). - 0.1: too broad: generic common noun or category, such as board game, leader, or money, that cannot identify the requested referent. - 0.2: specific, real entity of the same type the riddle asks for that fits some of the clues, plausible near miss. - 0.3: hallucinated or irrelevant: an invented entity, or real entity or word that does not fit the clues or is of the wrong type. This is the most common incorrect category; use it whenever the answer is not plausible near miss. - 0.4: another incorrect answer, including word or phrase copied from the riddle that shows no progress toward the answer; explain it in validator_note. score of 0 always takes 0.x category and score of 2 always takes 2.x category. If your category and score disagree, change the category. Return only the JSON object required by the structured output schema.
